{{nihongo|'''Ooyama Shrine'''|大山神社 (西ノ島町)}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Oki Province]].

}}'''Oyama Shrine'' (Oyama Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|Q132751|qid=Q132751}}{{ill|Oki District, Shimane|Q735735|qid=Q735735}}{{ill|Nishinoshima, Shimane|Q543193|qid=Q543193}}. {{ill|Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikiuchi-sha}} is located at the north foot of {{ill|Mount Takuhi|ceb|Takuhi Yama|ja|焼火山|ko|다쿠히산|lld|Takuhiyama|qid=Q11567667}}, the highest peak of {{ill|Dozen|qid=Dozen|lt=Dozen}}, to the east of Otsu village. It had a close relationship with {{ill|Takuhi Shrine|ja|焼火神社|qid=Q11567668}}, which was widely worshiped as {{ill|Guardian deities|ja|守護神|qid=Q131278957}} and was enshrined on the slope of Yakevolcano.

=== Enshrined God ===
*{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Mikoto Oyama}}
Although I don't see any particular theories, it is said that the yakivolcano that was originally called ``Oyama'' was {{ill|Shintai|Q327532|qid=Q327532}} ({{ill|Sacred mountains|ar|جبال مقدسة|ca|Muntanyes sagrades|de|Heiliger Berg|es|Montaña sagrada|fa|کوه‌های مقدس|fi|Pyhä vuori|fr|Montagne sacrée|id|Gunung keramat|ja|神体山|lt|Alkakalnis|lv|Svētie kalni|pl|Święte góry|ru|Священная гора|sq|Malet e shenjta|uk|Священна гора|vi|Núi thiêng|qid=Q1595289}}), and that the mountain itself was worshiped {{sfn|Edited by Shikinaisha Research Group|1983}}. This god and {{ill|Ujika Shrine|ja|宇受賀命神社|qid=Q11449116|lt=Usukega no Mikoto}} visit {{ill|Hinamajihimemikoto Shrine|ja|比奈麻治比売命神社|qid=Q133940165|lt=Hinamajhime no Mikoto}} There is a tradition that Uukega no Mikoto won due to the interference of {{ill|Amanojaku|ca|Ama-no-jaku|es|Ama-no-jaku|fa|آمانوجاکو|fr|Amanojaku|id|Amanojaku|it|Amanojaku|ja|天邪鬼|ko|아마노자쿠|pl|Amanjaku|pt|Amanojaku|ru|Аманодзяку|uk|Аманоджяку|vi|Amanojaku|zh|天邪鬼|zh_yue|天邪鬼|qid=Q2417460}}.{{sfn|Nagami|1968|p=628}} After that, {{ill|Mount Takuhi|ceb|Takuhi Yama|ja|焼火山|ko|다쿠히산|lld|Takuhiyama|qid=Q11567667}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Iekatsuyama}} (Atodo-san) competed again over {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sakaki}}, and this time it was Heaven. It is said that the demons got in the way of Uukega no Mikoto, resulting in the victory of the god of Oyama, and as a result, sakaki trees flourished on Yakivolcano, but no sakaki trees grew on Mt. Ietaka {{sfn|Nagami|1968|p=628}}. It is said that the two gods are not on good terms because of this kind of relationship.{{sfn|Nagami|1968|p=628}}.

=== History == =The date of its creation is unknown, but as mentioned above, it is believed that it was originally established as a shrine to enshrine Daisen (a volcanic volcano) as a sacred mountain. Furthermore, 200 meters west of the enshrinement site is the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hyogo Ruins}}, which appears to be a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=ritual ruins}} from the middle to late {{ill|Kofun period|Q459939|qid=Q459939}}, and it is assumed that water or spring rituals related to agriculture were held there, but its relationship with this shrine is unknown {{sfn|Heibonsha edition|1995}}.It was known in the central government from an early period, and is listed in "{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}" as a small shrine in {{ill|Oki Province|Q1063829|qid=Q1063829}}{{ill|Chibu district|Q11584565|qid=Q11584565}}. It is not known that the award of |Junior Third Rank |Q11591025}} is known, but in the ``{{ill|Izumi Province Divine Name Register|ja|国内神名帳|qid=Q11420490|lt=Inshu Shinto Name Book}}'' there is no rank called ``Junior Third Rank Upper<small>(Mama)</small>{{efn|Junior Third Rank Upper. }} Daisen Myojin” is written there. On the other hand, the shrine side (Negishiki side) has also been concerned about the current Mita area, which is centered on the enshrinement area, since it was organized into {{ill|Manorialism|Q1550557|qid=Q1550557}} and became {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Mita-sho}} (also called {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Mita-in}}), by directly connecting with the shugo power. It is said that this is where the close relationship between the two arose, with the intention of escaping from the ruling system.{{sfn|Edited by Heibonsha|1995}}{{efn|In addition, Mita-sho is thought to be a manor established in the eastern half of Nishinoshima, centered around present-day Mita, Nishinoshima-cho, extending from Beppu in the east to Uragato in the west. }}. However, this relationship underwent a major change around {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanbokucho period}}, and {{ill|Kenmu|Q1193970|qid=Q1193970|lt=In the first year of Kenmu}} ({{ill|1334|Q6007|qid=Q6007}}), the {{ill|Daikan|Q10263740|qid=Q10263740}} of Nishiryo and { Doken of {jalink|Kumon|Q11392042}}, at the behest of his feudal lord, set aside a part of Shonai as ``Oyamamiya Negibun Koushi (malt) rice farm.'' “Koshiryoba” is {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Divine sake}} It appears to be {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=hatake}} for supplying {{ill|Kōji (food)|Q865501|qid=Q865501|lt=koji}} for brewing {{sfn|edited by Heibonsha|1995}}. }}, a situation appeared where Mitashō was being incorporated under the control, and in {{ill|Ōan|Q1146245|qid=Q1146245}}2 ({{ill|1369|Q6211|qid=Q6211}}) The post of Negi, which became vacant after Renjo's death, was given to Doken Kumon, so <ref> ``Certain {{ill|ateokonaijō|Q11388108|qid=Q11388108}}'' (Kasagi family document) dated June 24, 2011. </ref>, it is assumed that it was completely incorporated into Mitasho, and after this point no documents related to this shrine can be seen, and the fact that related documents from before that have been handed down to the Kasagi clan, who are thought to be descendants of Doken (current Kasagi family documents), is thought to indicate this {{sfn|Edited by Heibonsha|1995}}.The subsequent history is not made clear, but in the early modern period it seems to have been subsumed into Unjo-ji Temple, which was called "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yakikazan Daigongen}}", and although the Kasagi clan held the {{ill|Kannushi (disambiguation)|Q15888735|qid=Q15888735|lt=Shinto Priest}}, Unjo-ji Temple was in charge as a Bettoto. (Unit)|Q855048|stone}} "Oki Kokishu" of 1823, which is said to have been {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sharyo}}<ref>{{ill|Bunsei|Q1327119|qid=Q1327119}}. </ref> is actually {{ill|Chigyō|Q11584648|qid=Q11584648}} of Unjouji Temple, and it was finally realized that the ``Oyama God'' was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yakebi Gongen}} (Unjouji Temple). {{sfn|Edited by Shikinai Society Research Group|1983}}{{efn|As an example of the view of Oyama no Kami as Yakibi Gongen, {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} 7th year (1667) '{ {jalink|Inshu Jōgoki|Q11659057}}'' says, ``Azuruni (Engishiki) Shinto name book, there is Oyama Shrine in Chibu district, this is the god of fire on the mountain (original Chinese)'', and ``{{jalin k|Dainihonshi|Q1156003|Dainipponshiji Jingishi}}, there is a statement that says, ``Oyama Shrine is located on the top of the Yakivolcano mountain in Hashimura, Imamida-go, and is called Yakihi Myojin (original Chinese).'' }}.

In the first year of {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}}, {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535}}, the shrine separated from Yakibi Gongen, and the official name of the shrine was ``Oyama Shrine'' according to the ``Engishiki'' ceremony, and in the 5th year of the Meiji era ({{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}}), it became a village shrine.

=== Rituals ===

=== Shinto ritual ===
In "Inshu Fudoki" written in {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}} 4 ({{ill|1833|Q7587|qid=Q7587}}), the festival dates are February 13th and June 14th, but after the implementation of {{ill|Solar calendar|Q210953|qid=Q210953}}, the current regular festival day is July 13th.

=== Priest ===
After the Middle Ages, the Betto-shoku of Unjo-ji Temple also served as the Negi-shoku, but in the late period, it is thought that the Kasagi family {{sfn|Edited by Heibonsha|1995}}, which seems to have taken on the Kumon-shoku of Mitashō, came to attack the Negi-shoku.In the early modern period, when Unjo-ji Temple became widely revered, Although the Kasagi family, who was in charge of the temple and served as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōshoya}}, called themselves ``Shinto priests'', their actual involvement was limited to {{ill|dānapati|Q11544585|qid=Q11544585}} {{sfn|Edited by Shikinaisha Research Group|1983}}. When the Meiji era policy of separating Shinto and Buddhism was carried out, in 1888, the betto of Unjo-ji Temple became {{ill|laicization in Buddhism|Q2583238|qid=Q2583238}} and became the priest (currently {{ill|Gūji|Q11453500|qid=Q11453500}}) using the surname Matsuura, and since then the Matsuura clan has inherited the position of chief priest.

=== Shrine building ===
{{ill|Honden|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994}} is 1 room long and has a {{ill|kōhai|Q11415970|qid=Q11415970}} of {{ill|Bargeboard|Q4881511|qid=Q4881511|lt=kara gable}} on the front. It is similar to |Q3193781}}, but the facing bow is a Karahafu and its width is narrower than the width of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=main building}} roof), and {{ill|chigi and katsuogi|Q87220234|qid=Q87220234}} is placed on the {{ill|ridge|qid=ridge|lt=ridge}}. Rebuilt in 1899. A passage hall with 1 beam and 3 beams extends from the bottom of the worship hall, and continues with the {{ill|Haiden (Shinto)|Q3125745|qid=Q3125745}} with 5 beams and 4 beams. All have roofs {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=copper plate}}.

The {{ill|Torii|Q234731|qid=Q234731}} located down the stone steps in front of the shrine is {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=made ​​of granite}} from {{ill|Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001}}12 ({{ill|1699|Q7710|qid=Q7710}}). It is the second oldest stone torii gate on Oki Island.

There is also a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shinsensho}} and a Mikoshi storehouse that stores {{ill|Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940}}.
